blocks.heading: Why small firms can survive
blocks.text: Small firms can survive by meeting needs that large suppliers cannot serve profitably or flexibly. A narrow local market may support a small repairer but not a large branch. Personal service can help an owner learn customer preferences, adjust an order quickly and win repeat business. A specialist may make customised goods that do not suit a standard production line. Close contact between owner, workers and customers can shorten decisions. Low overhead commitments may also help, although a small firm does not automatically have a lower cost per unit. Large rivals may obtain purchasing advantages if orders are sufficiently large and coordination remains effective. Small firms face disadvantages such as limited finance, dependence on a few customers and the owner’s limited time. Survival therefore requires enough demand and revenue to cover costs, not merely being friendly. Some owners deliberately remain small to preserve control and a manageable workload. Others are newly established businesses that may later grow. Judge survival against the actual customers and resources: a niche can protect a small supplier, but losing a major customer can make that niche too narrow.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nela Stitch, a three-person workshop in Keetmanshoop, alters individual garments within a day. A large clothing outlet nearby sells standard sizes and does not offer alterations. Nela serves a distinct tertiary service need with flexible personal attention. Customers needing a specific fit may pay for that convenience. Survival still depends on sufficient alteration orders to cover rent and wages; large retail sales nearby do not guarantee Nela’s demand.
